sections.model_projection: The model projects Missouri 28.72, Kansas 24.18, a margin of Missouri by 4.54 points. The projected total is 52.91, sitting 2.4 points above the current market number of 50.5. Missouri's win probability is 61.6% per the model, compared to the market-implied 65.75% for Missouri based on current money-line pricing.
sections.offensive_matchup: Kansas holds a clear edge in the passing game offensively, ranking 13th in opponent-adjusted passing EPA per play (0.458) against a Missouri pass defense that ranks 5th in the same metric (-0.036 allowed), creating a genuine clash of strengths. Missouri's defense has been elite at limiting success rate — allowing opponents to gain positive expected value on only 29% of plays (3rd nationally) — which directly threatens Kansas's ability to sustain drives. On the ground, Kansas's rushing offense (19th in opponent-adjusted rushing EPA at 0.230) faces a Missouri run defense that is merely average (44th, allowing +0.027 EPA per rush), giving the Jayhawks a modest but real advantage in the run game. Missouri's own offense is more balanced, ranking 34th in overall offensive EPA per play (0.249) but leaning heavily run-heavy with a neutral-script pass rate of just 44% (110th), which may limit their ceiling against a Kansas defense that has been stout.
sections.quarterback_edge: Kansas's Isaiah Marshall is flagged as a new starter at the same program with only 22 career attempts and one qualifying game, making his sample too thin for a reliable EPA-based evaluation; the model falls back to team passing EPA to assess this edge. Missouri's Austin Simmons is a transfer starter with 120 career attempts across five qualifying games, a career yards-per-attempt of 9.83, and a career completion rate of 63.3%, giving him a meaningful experience advantage over Marshall. Marshall's raw numbers from his one start are eye-catching — 77.3% completion rate and 12.45 yards per attempt — but the tiny sample warrants caution. The model scores this edge modestly in Kansas's favor (+0.66 points toward home) largely because Marshall's team-level passing EPA in Week 1 was exceptional, but the experience gap is real and could matter in a road-environment game for Simmons.
sections.trenches: Kansas's defensive front is the most decisive unit on the field, ranking 7th in opponent-adjusted havoc rate (14.0% of plays producing a disruption) and 7th in line yards allowed (2.06 per rush), while Missouri's offensive line allowed a sack on 5.8% of dropbacks (82nd nationally) and generated only middling havoc allowed (62nd). That combination — a dominant Kansas front against a Missouri line that struggles to protect — is the single largest positive edge for Kansas in the model, worth roughly 1.1 points. On the other side, Kansas's offensive line is excellent at protecting its quarterback, ranking 4th in opponent-adjusted havoc allowed (5.7%) and 4th in line yards generated (3.62), while Missouri's pass rush ranks 19th in sack rate (8.4%) — a credible threat but not dominant enough to fully neutralize Kansas's protection. The trench battle slightly favors Kansas overall, particularly in how their defensive front can disrupt Missouri's run-heavy attack.
sections.explosive_play_edge: This matchup is essentially a wash in the explosive-play dimension, with the model scoring it near zero. Missouri's offense generates explosive plays (10+ rush, 20+ pass) on 15.1% of plays (18th), while Kansas's defense has allowed them on 10.1% (36th) — a slight Missouri disadvantage. Kansas's offense produces explosives at a 15.7% rate (9th), and Missouri's defense has allowed them on only 8.2% of plays (13th), partially neutralizing Kansas's big-play capability. Neither team is likely to win this game on chunk plays alone; sustained efficiency will matter more.
sections.third_down_red_zone: Missouri holds a meaningful edge on third down, converting at 49.1% (13th) while holding opponents to just 30.5% (12th) — a double-sided advantage that should translate to longer drives and more defensive stops. Kansas converts third downs at only 44.6% (32nd) and allows opponents to convert at 35.1% (45th), a noticeably weaker profile on both sides. In the red zone, both teams' data carry low-sample flags after one game, so treat these numbers with caution; Missouri's 80.1% red-zone touchdown rate and 5.93 points per scoring opportunity (1st in the blend) suggest strong finishing ability, while Kansas's defense has allowed touchdowns on 54.5% of red-zone trips. Missouri's ability to convert opportunities into touchdowns rather than field goals could be a decisive factor if the game is close.
sections.roster_talent: Missouri holds a substantial talent advantage, with a recruiting talent percentile of 86 and a four-year blue-chip ratio of 36%, compared to Kansas's 54th-percentile talent and a blue-chip ratio of just 6%. This gap is the single largest driver in the model, contributing roughly -5.45 points toward Kansas. Missouri also has higher roster continuity (44% vs. 33%) and more returning production overall (37% vs. 25%), though Kansas returns more on defense (53% vs. 33%). Kansas's low returning production on offense — just 7% at passing and 9% at rushing — is a meaningful concern heading into a game against a talented SEC opponent.
sections.recent_form: Both teams have played exactly one game, so recent form is based entirely on Week 1 results with no trend data available. Missouri scored 54 points and allowed 14 in their opener, while Kansas scored 51 and allowed 6. Both performances look dominant in raw terms, but both faced opponents ranked 130th or worse in strength of schedule, so the numbers should be interpreted cautiously. The model assigns no form-based edge to either team given the identical one-game baseline.
sections.market_movement: The spread opened at Kansas +7.0 and has moved 1.5 points toward Kansas, landing at +5.5 on DraftKings. That move crosses the key number of 7, which historically carries more significance than a simple 1.5-point shift implies. The total moved in the opposite direction, dropping 2.0 points from 52.5 to 50.5. The model's projected margin of Missouri -4.54 sits about 1.0 point closer to Kansas than the current market spread of -5.5, and the model's total of 52.91 is 2.4 points above the market number of 50.5. Public betting percentages are unavailable, so no claim is made about what drove these moves.
key_advantages: Missouri's defense ranks 3rd in opponent success rate allowed (29.1%) and 5th in defensive passing EPA, making it one of the most efficient units in the country at preventing positive plays
Missouri's talent edge is significant — 86th-percentile recruiting vs. Kansas's 54th, with a blue-chip ratio six times larger
Kansas's defensive front ranks 7th in havoc rate and 7th in line yards allowed, posing a real threat to Missouri's run-heavy, average-protection offensive line
Kansas's home-field advantage is worth approximately 6.1 points in the model, the largest single factor working in the Jayhawks' favor
key_concerns: Kansas's quarterback Isaiah Marshall has only 22 career attempts, creating significant uncertainty about how he performs in a higher-stakes environment against an elite Missouri defense
Kansas returns only 7% of passing production and 9% of rushing production, the lowest continuity figures in the key skill positions for either team
Missouri's offensive line ranks 82nd in sack rate allowed, a vulnerability that Kansas's top-10 defensive front is well-positioned to exploit
Both teams' red-zone and scoring-opportunity metrics carry low-sample flags after one game, reducing confidence in those specific projections
sections.expected_game_script: Missouri figures to control the line of scrimmage defensively, holding Kansas to short gains and forcing the Jayhawks into third-and-medium situations where their 44.6% conversion rate becomes a liability against Missouri's 12th-ranked third-down defense. Kansas's defensive front, however, should make life uncomfortable for Missouri's offense, particularly on early downs where Missouri's run-heavy approach (44% neutral-script pass rate) runs directly into a Kansas front that ranks 7th in line yards allowed. The result is likely a game where both offenses grind rather than explode, consistent with the model's total projection of 52.9 — slightly above the market's 50.5. Missouri's superior talent and defensive efficiency should allow them to win the turnover-neutral possession battle, converting drives at a higher rate given their 49.1% third-down offense versus Kansas's 35.1% third-down defense allowed. Kansas's best path to an upset runs through Isaiah Marshall finding the intermediate passing game — their passing offense ranked 13th in opponent-adjusted EPA — against a Missouri secondary that, while elite, has not yet faced a quarterback with Marshall's efficiency numbers. Home field and the crowd at Memorial Stadium provide Kansas a real structural boost worth roughly 6 points, keeping this game competitive deep into the fourth quarter even if Missouri controls most of the statistical edges.
